summary: Animal nutrition for 7–8 year-olds (UK DfE Y3 'Animals, including humans'). The load-bearing idea is that plants MAKE their own food using light while animals CANNOT and must EAT to get energy and nutrients. From there children sort foods into the food groups of a local healthy-eating guide (in the UK, the Eatwell Guide's five groups), learn separately which nutrients foods supply and what each does for the body (energy, growth/repair, warmth, health, gut function; water for hydration), recognising that most foods supply several nutrients, and grasp that the body needs the RIGHT TYPES and RIGHT AMOUNTS — a variety of foods from each food group in roughly the guide's proportions over a day or week, not a single favourite or simply 'more'. Consequences of imbalance (weak bones without calcium, illness without vitamin C) make this concrete. The core proposed activity is a build-a-balanced-plate task with a responsive balance meter, complemented by a real classroom food-sort and a plant-vs-animal contrast that also links to food chains; alternatives (reveal poster, sorting consolidation, nutritionist dialogue) are kept for their distinct purposes.
misconceptions: Thinking animals (or humans) can make their own food or 'get energy from the sun' like plants — the core misconception this topic must correct.
Believing 'more food is always better' or that one favourite food can be a whole diet, missing 'right amounts' and variety.
Assuming each food supplies just one nutrient, rather than most foods supplying several (e.g. milk supplies protein, fat and calcium).

Calling nutrients (carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins) 'food groups' — food groups are groups of foods on a healthy-eating guide such as the Eatwell Guide, and each food supplies several nutrients.
Confusing 'healthy = expensive/special food' rather than balance across ordinary foods.
Thinking only 'unhealthy' people need to worry about nutrition, rather than everyone needing the right types and amounts.

activities.title: Build a balanced plate with a live balance meter
steps: Drag on-screen food cards onto an Eatwell-style plate divided into the five food groups while a health/balance meter responds to what you add (in the classroom, do a parallel hands-on sort using real packets and pictures of your own meals).
Pile the plate with only cakes and sweets and read the meter: it swings to 'too much sugar — not enough for growth', with a cartoon body looking sluggish.

Now swap in foods from the main food groups — fruit and vegetables, a starchy food such as bread or rice, a protein food such as beans, eggs or fish, and a dairy food such as yoghurt — with water to drink; watch the meter settle into the green as the body perks up.
Compare two plates with the SAME total amount of food but different variety, and say which scores healthier and why.
When a nutrient is missing, read the consequence pop-up (e.g. too little calcium over a long time → weak bones; too little vitamin C over a long time → illness) and add a food that fixes it.
activities.insight: It is the right TYPES and AMOUNTS together — a variety of foods from each food group in roughly the guide's proportions — that keep the body healthy, not quantity alone; the same total food scores differently depending on its variety.

activities.title: Plant makes food vs animal must eat
steps: Watch or act out two side-by-side cases: a plant in sunlight whose food bar fills on its own, and an animal whose hunger bar only refills when you feed it.
Toggle sunlight on and off: the plant's food bar fills only when light is on, while the animal's hunger bar does not respond to sunlight at all.
Feed the animal a meal and watch its hunger bar refill, then say in your own words why the animal needed the food.
Answer: 'Can a dog just sit in the sun and make its own food like a sunflower?' and explain where the dog's energy actually comes from.
Trace a food chain: a cow eats grass and a lion eats the cow — say how each gets its energy, and where the energy in a slice of bread first came from (the plant, which captured it from the sun).
activities.insight: Animals cannot make their own food and must eat (plants or other animals) to get energy and nutrients; plants make their own food using light, and in food chains like these the energy animals eat traces back to plants.

activities.title: Reveal-the-job nutrients and food-groups poster (scaffold)
steps: Tap or lift each flap of a nutrients poster to reveal the nutrient and its job (carbohydrates for energy, protein for growth/repair, fats for energy/warmth, vitamins & minerals for health, fibre for the gut, water for everything).
Tap each section of an Eatwell plate panel to reveal the food group's name and two example foods.
Open a myth-buster flap: 'Can animals make their own food like plants?' and read the answer.
Name a food you ate recently, say which food group it belongs to and which nutrients it supplies.
activities.insight: Each nutrient has a job in the body; food groups sort foods on a healthy-eating guide, and each food supplies several nutrients.

activities.title: Sort-and-match consolidation
steps: Sort a set of food cards into the Eatwell Guide's five food groups, using a 'mixed foods' pile for dishes such as pizza that combine several groups.
Match each nutrient (carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, fibre, plus water) to its function, and name a food that supplies several of them (e.g. milk or an egg).
Answer 'why can't a cat make its own food?' and explain in a sentence.
Spot and reject a wrong claim such as 'humans make food from sunlight'.
activities.insight: Consolidate sorting foods into food groups, linking nutrients to their functions, and the reason animals cannot make their own food.

activities.title: Ask-a-nutritionist curiosity dialogue
steps: Ask a nutritionist/'body' character questions such as 'What happens if I only eat chips?', 'Is more food always better?' and 'Why can't I make my own food?'.
Predict the answer before revealing it, then compare.
Use the answer to plan one change to a one-sided plate.
activities.insight: A one-sided or over-large diet causes problems; the body needs variety and the right amounts, and animals must eat to get nutrients.

checkQuestion: A plant can sit in the sunshine and make its own food. Can a dog do the same — just sit in the sun and make its own food? Explain why or why not, and where a dog's energy actually comes from.
checkAnswer: No — animals like the dog cannot make their own food; they must EAT food (plants or other animals) to get energy and nutrients. Only plants can make their own food using sunlight. The dog's energy comes from the food it eats, which is why animals must find and eat food to survive.
